blocks.html: In Our Neighbors: Canada and Mexico you found the three big countries of North America. Now zoom in on the middle one: the United States. Where exactly is it, and what is around it?

The United States is in North America. Canada is to the north, Mexico is to the south, the Atlantic Ocean is to the east and the Pacific Ocean is to the west. Alaska is in the far northwest, and Hawaii is out in the Pacific.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: North America. The United States is orange. Find Alaska in the top left corner, next to Canada.

blocks.html: Why use neighbors to describe a place? A location is easiest to remember when you tie it to things around it. "Between Canada and Mexico, from the Atlantic to the Pacific" tells anyone in the world where to look, even without a map. This is called relative location.

blocks.title: Describe the location
blocks.q: A pen pal in Japan asks where the United States is. What could you say?
steps: Start with the continent: North America.
Name the neighbors: Canada to the north and Mexico to the south.
Name the oceans: the Atlantic to the east and the Pacific to the west.
Add the two far-away states: Alaska in the northwest and Hawaii in the Pacific.
blocks.a: "The United States is in North America, between Canada and Mexico, from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific."

blocks.html: Many U.S. maps put Alaska and Hawaii in small boxes near Mexico, just to save space. That makes some people think Alaska is a small island near Mexico. It is not. Alaska is joined to North America in the far northwest, next to Canada, and it is the largest state. Check the inset: if a map has boxes, read them as "moved here to fit."

blocks.html: A country can be split into smaller parts. In the United States those parts are called states. You met them in The United States and Its States. Here is the whole picture.
The United States has 50 states and the District of Columbia (Washington, D.C.), the nation's capital. 48 states touch one another in one block of land. Alaska and Hawaii stand apart.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Tap any state to see its name, its capital and when it joined.

blocks.html: Why is the capital not in a state? When the Constitution was written, its authors wanted the national government to sit on land that no single state controlled, so no state would have extra power over it. Maryland and Virginia gave land along the Potomac River, and the District of Columbia was made there. It belongs to the whole country.

blocks.title: Counting the block of 48
blocks.q: How many states touch at least one other state?
steps: There are 50 states in all.
Alaska touches only Canada. Hawaii is surrounded by ocean.

blocks.html: Washington, D.C., is not in Washington State. They share a name (both honor George Washington) but sit on opposite sides of the country. Washington State is in the far northwest. Washington, D.C., is on the East Coast, between Maryland and Virginia. D.C. is also not a state: it is a federal district.

blocks.html: The 50 states and D.C. are not the whole United States. The country also has territories: places that belong to the United States but are not states.

The five territories where people live are Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands in the Caribbean Sea, and Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa in the Pacific Ocean. They are part of the United States, but they are not states.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The five territories where people live: two in the Caribbean, three in the Pacific.

blocks.html: How is a territory different from a state? A state has two senators and voting members in the House of Representatives. A territory has no senators, and its one member of the House cannot vote on passing laws. Each territory has its own local government, and the U.S. government is responsible for its defense.

blocks.cap: People born in American Samoa are U.S. nationals: they may live and work anywhere in the United States, and may apply to become citizens.

blocks.title: Territory or not?
blocks.q: Is Hawaii a territory?
steps: Hawaii became part of the United States in 1898 and was a territory for many years.
In 1959 it became the 50th state.
So today it is a state, not a territory.

blocks.html: Some people think Puerto Rico is a separate country, and others think it is a state. It is neither. Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory, and people born there are U.S. citizens. They can move to any state and live there like anyone else.

blocks.html: Fifty states are a lot to learn at once. Geographers make it easier by grouping states that are near each other into regions.
The U.S. Census Bureau divides the states into four regions: the Northeast, the Midwest, the South and the West. Inside them are nine smaller divisions, such as New England and the Pacific.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The Census Bureau's four regions.

blocks.html: Why group states? States near each other often share land, weather, history and ways of making a living. Grouping them lets you learn a few at a time and compare one part of the country with another. The Census Bureau uses its regions to report facts about people, so many maps and charts use them too.

blocks.title: Which region?
blocks.q: Is Maryland in the Northeast or the South?
steps: Maryland is just south of Pennsylvania, on Chesapeake Bay.
The Census Bureau puts it in the South Atlantic division.
So, by the Census Bureau, Maryland is in the South.

blocks.html: Students expect one official way to divide the country. There isn't one. Many textbooks use five regions, adding a Southeast and a Southwest, and some put Maryland or Delaware in the Northeast. This ladder uses the Census Bureau's four regions and nine divisions. Delaware, Maryland, West Virginia, Kentucky, Oklahoma and Texas surprise people: all are in the South.

blocks.html: Look at any envelope with an American address. After the city comes a two-letter code, like TX or NY, then the ZIP Code. Those are postal codes.
Every state has a two-letter postal code, written in capital letters with no period: CA for California, TX for Texas, NY for New York. D.C. is DC.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Every state with its postal code.

blocks.html: Why two letters? In 1963 the Post Office brought in five-digit ZIP Codes. The machines that printed addresses could fit only about 23 characters on the last line, so long state names had to shrink. The Post Office gave every state a two-letter code that no other state shares. (Nebraska was NB at first; it became NE in 1969 so it would not be confused with New Brunswick in Canada.)

blocks.title: The M states
blocks.q: Eight states start with M. What are their codes?
steps: Maine ME, Maryland MD, Massachusetts MA.
Michigan MI, Minnesota MN.
Mississippi MS, Missouri MO, Montana MT.
Notice that only MA, MI and MO follow a simple rule; the rest use a later letter.
blocks.a: ME, MD, MA, MI, MN, MS, MO, MT.

blocks.html: Guessing from the first two letters goes wrong for states that share a start. AK is Alaska and AR is Arkansas (AL is Alabama, AZ is Arizona). IA is Iowa, ID Idaho, IL Illinois, IN Indiana. MI is Michigan, not Mississippi (MS) or Missouri (MO). Learn the look-alikes as a group.

blocks.html: Start in the Northeast, the corner of the country where the first English colonies grew. It has small states packed close together, so take them slowly.

The Northeast has nine states: the six New England states (Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Connecticut) and the three Middle Atlantic states (New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania).

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The states of this region, with their names.

blocks.html: Why are these states so small? They began as colonies whose borders were drawn in the 1600s and 1700s, when people traveled on foot, by horse or by boat. A state you could cross in a day or two made sense then. Western states were drawn much later, with long straight lines over huge, open land.

items: Maine is the big state in the far northeast corner.
Vermont and New Hampshire are a pair of thin states: Vermont is wider at the top, New Hampshire wider at the bottom.
Massachusetts runs across the middle, with Cape Cod curling out like an arm.
Rhode Island (the smallest state) and Connecticut sit below Massachusetts.
New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania form the Middle Atlantic, west and south of New England.

blocks.title: Find Connecticut
blocks.q: Which state is directly south of Massachusetts and west of Rhode Island?
steps: South of Massachusetts are two small states: Connecticut and Rhode Island.
Rhode Island is the eastern one, the smallest state.
So the western one, next to New York, is Connecticut.

blocks.html: Vermont and New Hampshire look like the same shape flipped. Here is the check: New Hampshire touches the ocean (a short coast) and borders Maine. Vermont touches New York and has no ocean coast. Say it as "Vermont is next to New York; New Hampshire is next to Maine."

blocks.html: You can find the nine Northeastern states. Now learn the city where each one's government meets.

The Northeast's capitals: Augusta (Maine), Concord (New Hampshire), Montpelier (Vermont), Boston (Massachusetts), Providence (Rhode Island), Hartford (Connecticut), Albany (New York), Trenton (New Jersey) and Harrisburg (Pennsylvania).

blocks.html: A capital is the city where a state's government meets: the governor works there and the legislature writes laws there. Many capitals were chosen long ago because they were near the middle of the state, easy for lawmakers to reach by horse or riverboat. The biggest cities often grew later, around ports and railroads. That is why the capital is so often not the biggest city.

blocks.title: New York's capital
blocks.q: What is the capital of New York?
steps: New York City is the biggest city in the country, so it is tempting.
But the state government meets upstate, on the Hudson River.
That city is Albany.

blocks.html: The biggest-city trap: New York's capital is Albany, not New York City, and Pennsylvania's is Harrisburg, not Philadelphia or Pittsburgh. Boston and Providence are the two capitals here that are also their state's biggest city.

Memory help. Montpelier, Vermont, is the smallest state capital by population. Hartford, Connecticut, and Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, both start with H; picture Harrisburg on the Susquehanna River in the middle of Pennsylvania.

blocks.html: Next comes the Midwest, the farm and factory heartland between the Appalachians and the Rockies.

The Midwest has twelve states. The East North Central states are Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan and Wisconsin, around the Great Lakes. The West North Central states are Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska and Kansas, on the plains.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The states of this region, with their names.

blocks.html: Why are so many Midwestern borders straight lines? Much of this land was surveyed in a grid of squares before most settlers arrived, so lawmakers drew borders along lines of latitude and longitude. Where a river was handy, they used it: the Mississippi separates Iowa and Missouri from Illinois and Wisconsin.

items: Michigan is the mitten, with its upper peninsula above it.
Ohio, Indiana and Illinois line up west of Pennsylvania, south of the Great Lakes.
Minnesota is at the top, next to Lake Superior and Canada.
Iowa sits above Missouri, between the Mississippi and the Missouri rivers.
The Dakotas, Nebraska and Kansas stack from north to south on the Great Plains.

blocks.title: Stack the plains states
blocks.q: From north to south, which four states line up in a column on the Great Plains?
steps: Start at the Canadian border: North Dakota.
Below it: South Dakota.
Below that: Nebraska, then Kansas.
blocks.a: North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas.

blocks.html: Iowa and Missouri get switched, and so do Nebraska and Kansas. Two checks: Missouri is south of Iowa (Missouri touches Arkansas), and Kansas is directly south of Nebraska (Kansas touches Oklahoma). Nebraska has a notch cut out of its southwest corner; Kansas is a near-rectangle with a bite out of its northeast corner, where the Missouri River runs.

blocks.title: The Twin Cities
blocks.q: Minneapolis and Saint Paul sit side by side on the Mississippi. Which one is Minnesota's capital?
steps: Minneapolis is the larger of the two.
The state capitol building is across the river, in Saint Paul.
So Saint Paul is the capital.

blocks.html: Students pick the biggest city: Illinois's capital is Springfield, not Chicago; Michigan's is Lansing, not Detroit; Missouri's is Jefferson City, not Kansas City or St. Louis; Wisconsin's is Madison, not Milwaukee.

Memory help. Pierre, South Dakota, is said "peer." Two Midwest capitals are named for presidents: Lincoln (Nebraska) and Jefferson City (Missouri). Columbus, Ohio, and Indianapolis, Indiana, are both near the middle of their states.

blocks.html: The South is the biggest Census region, so we take it in two parts. First, the South Atlantic: the states along the coast from Delaware down to Florida.
The South Atlantic division has eight states, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, plus the District of Columbia.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The states of this region, with their names.

blocks.html: Why is West Virginia in a division named for the Atlantic when it has no coast? The Census Bureau groups states that are close together and share history. West Virginia was part of Virginia until 1863, so it stays in the same division as its old partner.

items: Delaware is the small state on the coast east of Maryland.
Maryland wraps around Chesapeake Bay; Washington, D.C., sits on its southwest edge.
Virginia is below Maryland, and West Virginia is the mountain state to its west.
North Carolina is long and wide; South Carolina is the triangle below it.
Georgia is next, and Florida is the long peninsula at the bottom.

blocks.title: Coast or no coast
blocks.q: Which South Atlantic state has no ocean coast?
steps: Go down the coast: Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida all touch the Atlantic.
West Virginia sits behind Virginia, in the mountains.

blocks.html: Students forget that Delaware, Maryland and West Virginia count as the South in the Census Bureau's regions. The Census groups them with the South Atlantic. Another mix-up: North and South Carolina. North Carolina is the bigger, wider one; South Carolina is the smaller triangle below it.

steps: Miami, Orlando and Tampa are famous, and Jacksonville is the largest city.

blocks.html: Now the rest of the South: the two South Central divisions, from Kentucky to Texas.

The South Central states are East South Central: Kentucky, Tennessee, Alabama and Mississippi; and West South Central: Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas. The Mississippi River splits the two divisions.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The states of this region, with their names.

blocks.html: Why does the Mississippi River split them? Big rivers were the highways of the 1800s, and they made easy borders to agree on. The Mississippi forms much of the line between Tennessee and Mississippi on the east and Arkansas and Louisiana on the west.

items: Kentucky is on top, with the Ohio River along its north edge; Tennessee is the long, thin state below it.
Mississippi and Alabama sit side by side below Tennessee.
Arkansas is west of the river; Louisiana, shaped like a boot, is below it.
Oklahoma, shaped like a pan with a handle, sits on top of Texas.

blocks.title: The boot
blocks.q: Which state is shaped like a boot, at the mouth of the Mississippi?
steps: Follow the Mississippi River south to the Gulf.
The last state it crosses has a boot shape, with the toe pointing east.

blocks.html: Alabama and Mississippi get switched because they sit side by side with similar shapes. Use the river: Mississippi is the western one, along the Mississippi River. Alabama is the eastern one, next to Georgia.

blocks.html: Head west into the West. Its first division, the Mountain states, follows the Rocky Mountains and the dry lands beside them.
The eight Mountain states are Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The states of this region, with their names.

blocks.html: Why so many boxes? These borders were drawn in Washington, D.C., in the 1800s, often before many settlers lived there. Lawmakers used lines of latitude and longitude, so Wyoming and Colorado came out as near-rectangles, and four states meet at one point, the Four Corners.

items: Montana is the big state on the Canadian border; Idaho is the narrow one west of it, with a thin handle at the top.
Wyoming sits below Montana; Colorado sits below Wyoming.
Nevada is the wedge next to California; Utah has a notch in its northeast corner.
Arizona and New Mexico are the southern pair: Arizona west, New Mexico east.

blocks.title: The Four Corners
blocks.q: Which four states meet at a single point?
steps: Find the corner where Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico come together.
It is the only place in the country where four states meet.
blocks.a: Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico.

blocks.html: Wyoming and Colorado are two near-rectangles, one above the other. Wyoming is the northern one, under Montana; Colorado touches New Mexico. Arizona and New Mexico are also a pair: Arizona is the western one, next to California and the Colorado River.

blocks.html: The last division of the West is the Pacific: the states that touch the Pacific Ocean.
The five Pacific states are Washington, Oregon and California along the West Coast, plus Alaska and Hawaii.

blocks.html: Why are Alaska and Hawaii grouped with the West Coast? Both touch the Pacific, and the Census Bureau groups states by the ocean and land they share. On most maps they appear in boxes near California for the same reason.

items: Washington is at the top, on the Canadian border, with Puget Sound cutting into it.
Oregon is in the middle.
California is the long state reaching down to Mexico.
Alaska is the giant in the northwest; Hawaii is the island chain in the middle of the Pacific.

blocks.title: Coast order
blocks.q: Driving south along the Pacific coast from Canada to Mexico, which states do you pass, in order?
steps: Start at the Canadian border: Washington.
Next: Oregon.
Last and longest: California.

blocks.html: You have learned the states region by region, from the Northeast to the Pacific. Now put the whole map together and find any state without the region to help.

To find a state on the full map, use anchors: big, easy states you know for sure (Texas, California, Florida, Michigan, Maine). Then work outward: "Oklahoma is the pan above Texas," "Nevada is next to California."

blocks.html: Why do anchors work? Your memory stores places as a web of neighbors, not as a list. When you link a hard state to an easy one ("Delaware is the small state east of Maryland"), finding one helps you find the other. That is also why it helps to learn shapes: a shape is a quick clue you can check.

blocks.title: Three square states
blocks.q: Colorado, Wyoming and Utah are all boxy. How can you tell which is which?
steps: Utah has a notch cut out of its top right corner.
Wyoming is the box under Montana.
Colorado is the box under Wyoming, above New Mexico.
blocks.a: Utah has the notch; Wyoming is north; Colorado is south.

blocks.html: Students who know states only inside their region lose them on the full map. The usual trouble spots are the small eastern states (Vermont and New Hampshire, Connecticut and Rhode Island, Delaware and Maryland) and the boxy western states (Wyoming, Colorado, the Dakotas). Zoom in on the East, and use a shape clue for each box.

blocks.html: You have learned capitals one region at a time. Now mix them all together. Mixing is harder, and it is the best way to make them stick.
Every state has one capital, where its government meets. Learn each capital together with its state's place on the map, and watch for capitals with look-alike names.

blocks.html: Why mix the regions? When you practice one region at a time, you already know which few answers are possible. Mixed practice makes you pick the right capital out of fifty, which is what you will need to do later. It feels harder, and that extra effort is what helps you remember.

blocks.q: Lansing is the capital of which state?
steps: Lansing is in the lower part of a mitten-shaped state.
Detroit is that state's biggest city, but not its capital.
The state is Michigan.

blocks.html: Names that sound alike trip people up: Columbia (South Carolina) and Columbus (Ohio); Charleston, which is West Virginia's capital and also a big city in South Carolina; and Jackson (Mississippi) and Jefferson City (Missouri). Tie each one to its state's place on the map.

blocks.html: Two states are neighbors when they share a border. Knowing neighbors helps you find states and understand how people, rivers and roads cross from one state to the next.
Neighboring states share a border along a line. Tennessee and Missouri each touch eight states, the most of any. Maine touches only one: New Hampshire. Alaska and Hawaii touch no other state.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Tennessee and its eight neighbors.

blocks.html: Why does Tennessee have so many neighbors? It is long and thin, stretching all the way from the Appalachians to the Mississippi River, so its edges run past many states. A long border on many sides means many neighbors. Maine sits in a corner with Canada on two sides and the ocean on the third, so only one state is left to touch.

blocks.title: Count Colorado's neighbors
blocks.q: How many states share a border with Colorado?
steps: North: Wyoming and Nebraska.
East: Kansas and the tip of Oklahoma.
South: New Mexico.
West: Utah.
Arizona touches Colorado only at a point, so it does not count.

blocks.html: At the Four Corners, Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico meet at one point. Arizona and Colorado touch only at that point, and so do Utah and New Mexico. A single point is not a shared border, so those pairs are not neighbors. Also, in this course a border means land: Michigan meets Minnesota only out in Lake Superior, so they are not counted as neighbors.

blocks.html: States are lines people drew. The land underneath has its own regions: places where the ground is alike. You know the landform words from Plains and Plateaus. Now see them across the whole country.

From east to west: the Coastal Plain, the Appalachian Mountains, the Central Lowland, the Great Plains, the Rocky Mountains, the high basins and plateaus (the Great Basin and the Colorado Plateau), and the Pacific mountains (the Sierra Nevada, the Cascades and the Coast Ranges).

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The landform regions. Tap a state to see where it sits.

blocks.html: Why are the eastern mountains low and the western ones high? Mountains form where pieces of Earth's crust push together, and then wind, water and ice slowly wear them down. The Appalachians rose hundreds of millions of years ago and have been wearing down ever since. The Rockies are much younger, so they are still tall and sharp. (Earth & Space explains how plates make mountains.)

blocks.title: A drive across the country
blocks.q: You drive west from Virginia Beach to Denver. What land do you cross?
steps: Virginia Beach is on the low, flat Coastal Plain.
You climb over the rounded Appalachian Mountains.
You cross the low, rolling farmland of the Central Lowland.
You climb gently across the flat Great Plains.
At Denver, the Rockies rise right in front of you.
blocks.a: Coastal Plain, Appalachians, Central Lowland, Great Plains, then the Rockies.

blocks.html: People picture the land rising evenly from the Atlantic to the Pacific, like a ramp. It does not. It rises into the Appalachians, drops into the Central Lowland, climbs slowly across the Great Plains (Denver, at their western edge, is about a mile high), and then shoots up into the Rockies. West of the Rockies come high deserts and more mountains before the Pacific.

blocks.cap: Low, old Appalachians in the East; tall, young Rockies in the West; the plains between.

blocks.html: In Landform Regions you met the big mountain regions. Now learn the ranges by name and where each one runs.

The Appalachians run near the East Coast, from Alabama to Maine. The Rockies run from New Mexico north through Colorado, Wyoming and Montana into Canada. Near the Pacific rise the Sierra Nevada (California), the Cascades (Washington, Oregon and northern California) and the Coast Ranges. Alaska has the Alaska Range and the Brooks Range.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The major mountain ranges.

blocks.html: Why do ranges run in long lines instead of round clumps? A range forms along the edge where two pieces of Earth's crust meet, or where one slides under another. That edge is a long line, so the mountains pushed up along it form a long line too. The Cascades are a line of volcanoes, such as Mount Rainier and Mount St. Helens, above a place where one plate sinks under another.

blocks.title: Which range?
blocks.q: Yosemite's granite cliffs and Mount Whitney are in which range?
steps: Both are in eastern California.
That is not the Rockies; it is a separate range near the Pacific.
It is the Sierra Nevada.

blocks.html: The Sierra Nevada is not part of the Rockies. It is its own range in California, with the Great Basin between it and the Rockies. And the Appalachians are in the East, not the West: if a range is near the Atlantic, it is the Appalachians.

blocks.html: Heights on a map are measured from sea level, the average level of the ocean. A place 100 feet above the ocean has an elevation of 100 feet. A place below the level of the ocean has a negative elevation.

Denali in Alaska is the highest peak in North America: 20,310 feet. Badwater Basin in Death Valley, California, is the lowest point in North America: 282 feet below sea level. The highest peak in the 48 states that touch one another is Mount Whitney in California's Sierra Nevada, about 14,500 feet.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The highest and lowest places, and the tallest peaks of the Rockies and the Appalachians.

blocks.html: How can land be below the ocean and stay dry? Death Valley is surrounded by mountains, so the ocean cannot flow in. The valley floor sank as the crust stretched and broke. Rain is rare, and the little water that runs in dries up in the heat, leaving salt flats.

blocks.title: Top to bottom
blocks.q: How many feet higher is the top of Denali (20,310 feet) than Badwater Basin (−282 feet)?
steps: From −282 up to sea level (0) is 282 feet.
From sea level up to 20,310 is 20,310 feet.

blocks.html: Many people guess the highest point is in the Rockies. The Rockies' tallest peak, Mount Elbert in Colorado, is about 14,400 feet. Denali, in the Alaska Range, is almost 6,000 feet higher. Even in the 48 states, the highest is Mount Whitney in the Sierra Nevada, not a Rocky Mountain peak. Denali's federal name has been Mount McKinley since 2025; Alaska and many others still call it Denali.
Fun fact: Mount Whitney and Badwater Basin are less than 85 miles apart, so the highest and lowest points of the 48 states are close neighbors.

blocks.html: In A River's Journey you saw that a river begins high up and flows downhill to the sea. So which sea? High in the Rockies runs a line that decides.

The Continental Divide runs along the high crests of the Rocky Mountains. Rain or snow that falls on its west side flows toward the Pacific Ocean. Water on its east side flows toward the Gulf of Mexico (since 2025 the U.S. federal government calls it the Gulf of America) and the Atlantic.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Rivers start in the Rockies and flow away on both sides: west to the Pacific, east to the Gulf.

blocks.html: Picture the roof of a house. Rain that lands on one side runs off that side; rain on the other side runs the other way. The ridge of the roof is the divide. The Continental Divide is the ridge of the continent: once water lands on one side, it can only run downhill, and downhill leads to one ocean or the other.

blocks.title: Two rivers from one state
blocks.q: The Colorado River and the Rio Grande both start in the Colorado Rockies. Where does each one go?
steps: The Colorado River starts on the west side of the Divide.
It flows southwest through the Grand Canyon toward the Gulf of California, an arm of the Pacific.
The Rio Grande starts on the east side.
It flows south through New Mexico and along the Texas-Mexico border to the Gulf.
blocks.a: The Colorado goes toward the Pacific; the Rio Grande goes to the Gulf.

blocks.html: People think rivers flow to the nearest ocean. They don't: they flow downhill. Water that falls just east of the Divide in Colorado is much closer to the Pacific than to the Gulf, but it still travels more than 1,000 miles east and south, because that is the way downhill goes. (A few places are exceptions, like the Great Divide Basin in Wyoming, where water collects and never reaches the sea.)

blocks.html: Rivers carried explorers, settlers and goods across the country long before railroads and highways. Many cities grew up on their banks.

The big rivers to know: the Mississippi (Minnesota to the Gulf), the Missouri (Montana to the Mississippi), the Ohio (Pittsburgh to the Mississippi), the Colorado (the Rockies through the Grand Canyon), the Columbia (the Washington-Oregon border to the Pacific) and the Rio Grande (Colorado to the Gulf, along the Texas-Mexico border).

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Major rivers. Some form borders between states.

blocks.html: Why do rivers make good borders? A river is easy to see and hard to argue about, so when states were drawn, lawmakers often used them. The Ohio River is Kentucky's whole northern border; the Columbia separates much of Washington from Oregon; the Rio Grande separates Texas from Mexico; and the Mississippi forms the edges of ten states.

blocks.title: A border river
blocks.q: Which river forms much of the border between Washington and Oregon?
steps: Find the two states in the far northwest.
A big river runs west along the line between them to the Pacific.
It is the Columbia.

blocks.html: Most people think the Mississippi is the longest U.S. river. By the U.S. Geological Survey's measure, the Missouri is a little longer, about 2,540 miles to the Mississippi's 2,340. The Missouri flows into the Mississippi, and together they make one of the longest river systems in the world, about 3,710 miles from the Missouri's source to the Gulf. (Different measurements give slightly different lengths.)

blocks.html: A big river is fed by smaller rivers, called tributaries. The Mississippi has the largest family of tributaries in North America.

The Missouri, Ohio and Arkansas rivers flow into the Mississippi, and the Tennessee flows into the Ohio. The Mississippi carries all of their water south to the Gulf of Mexico (since 2025 the U.S. federal government calls it the Gulf of America). All the land drained by this system is the river's basin.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The Mississippi and its big tributaries.

blocks.html: Why does one river collect so much? The middle of the country is a huge, shallow bowl between the Rockies and the Appalachians. Rain falling anywhere in the bowl runs downhill toward its lowest line, and that line is the Mississippi. The Continental Divide is the western rim of the bowl.

blocks.title: A raindrop's trip
blocks.q: A raindrop falls in western Pennsylvania. How does it reach the Gulf?
steps: It runs into a stream, then into a river that flows to Pittsburgh, where the Ohio River begins.
The Ohio flows west and joins the Mississippi at Cairo, Illinois.
The Mississippi carries it south, past New Orleans, to the Gulf.
blocks.a: Ohio River, then the Mississippi, then the Gulf.

blocks.html: People think a river's basin is just the river. The Mississippi's basin is all the land its tributaries drain: all or parts of 31 states and two Canadian provinces, about 40% of the lower 48 states, according to the National Park Service. A farm field in Montana and a parking lot in Pittsburgh are both in it.
The Mississippi starts at Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota. The Park Service says water leaving the lake takes about three months to reach the Gulf.

blocks.html: Along the border with Canada lie five huge freshwater lakes, so big that you cannot see across them. Ships sail on them, carrying iron ore, grain and coal.

The five Great Lakes are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario. Remember them with HOMES: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior. Lake Michigan is the only one entirely inside the United States; Canada shares the other four.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The Great Lakes, from Superior in the west to Ontario in the east.

blocks.html: Where did such big lakes come from? During the last ice age, thick sheets of ice covered this area. The moving ice scraped out deep basins, and when the ice melted, water filled them. Today the lakes drain east through the St. Lawrence River to the Atlantic.

blocks.title: West to east
blocks.q: Put the Great Lakes in order from west to east.
steps: Superior is the biggest, farthest north and west.
Michigan hangs down south of it; Huron lies east of Michigan.
Erie is south of Huron; Ontario is last, farthest east.

blocks.html: Many people think all five lakes belong to the United States. The U.S.-Canada border runs through the middle of Superior, Huron, Erie and Ontario. Only Lake Michigan lies wholly in the U.S., with Michigan, Wisconsin, Illinois and Indiana around it.

blocks.html: You learned bays, capes and peninsulas in Bays, Gulfs and Coasts. The U.S. coastline has famous examples of each.

The United States has three main coasts: the Atlantic (Maine to Florida), the Gulf (Florida to Texas, on the Gulf of Mexico (since 2025 the U.S. federal government calls it the Gulf of America)) and the Pacific (Washington to California, plus Alaska and Hawaii). Famous features include Chesapeake Bay, Cape Cod, the Florida Peninsula, Puget Sound and San Francisco Bay.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Bays, a cape and a peninsula on three coasts.

blocks.html: Why do so many big cities sit on bays? A bay is water partly wrapped by land, so its waves are calmer than the open ocean. Ships could anchor safely there, so ports grew: Baltimore on Chesapeake Bay, Boston near Cape Cod Bay, Seattle on Puget Sound, and San Francisco and Oakland on San Francisco Bay.

blocks.title: Two coasts
blocks.q: Which state has coastline on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf?
steps: A state would have to stick out between the two bodies of water.
The Florida Peninsula does just that.
Its east coast faces the Atlantic; its west coast faces the Gulf.

blocks.html: Students forget the Gulf coast. It is the long southern shore of Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas. Its body of water is the Gulf of Mexico; since 2025 the U.S. federal government calls it the Gulf of America. You may see either name on maps.

blocks.html: In Deserts, Forests and Grasslands you learned that a desert is a dry place. The United States has four big deserts, all in the West and Southwest.

The four big U.S. deserts are the Mojave (California and Nevada; Death Valley, Las Vegas, Joshua trees), the Sonoran (Arizona and California; saguaro cactus), the Chihuahuan (mostly in Mexico, reaching into New Mexico and West Texas) and the Great Basin (Nevada and Utah), a cold desert.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The four deserts. The Mojave sits between the Great Basin and the Sonoran.

blocks.html: Why is the West so dry? Storms come in from the Pacific. As the air rises over the Sierra Nevada and the Cascades, it cools and drops its rain and snow on the western slopes. By the time the air comes down the other side, it is dry. The land behind the mountains is in a rain shadow.

blocks.title: Match the plant
blocks.q: The tall saguaro cactus with arms grows in which desert?
steps: Saguaros need warm winters with little frost.
They grow in southern Arizona, around Phoenix and Tucson.
That is the Sonoran Desert.

blocks.html: Deserts are not always hot. A desert is defined by being dry. The Great Basin Desert is high and far north, so it has cold, snowy winters, yet it gets so little rain and snow in a year that it is still a desert.

blocks.html: The two newest states are unlike any others. One is huge and cold; the other is a chain of warm islands. Both joined in 1959.

Alaska is the largest state, with glaciers, tall mountains (including Denali) and tundra; its capital is Juneau and its biggest city is Anchorage. Hawaii is a chain of islands built by volcanoes in the middle of the Pacific; its capital, Honolulu, is on the island of Oahu.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Alaska in its real place, next to Canada, at the same scale as the 48 states.

blocks.html: How did volcanoes make Hawaii? Deep under the Pacific is a hot spot where melted rock rises. The Pacific plate slowly slides over it, and the hot spot builds one volcano after another, like a conveyor belt. The oldest islands are in the northwest; the island of Hawaii, in the southeast, is the youngest and still has active volcanoes.

blocks.title: How much bigger?
blocks.q: Alaska covers about 665,000 square miles and Texas about 269,000. About how many times as big is Alaska?
steps: That is about 2.5.
So Alaska is about two and a half times as big as Texas.

blocks.html: Small inset boxes on U.S. maps shrink Alaska to fit, so people think it is small. Alaska is more than twice as big as Texas, the second-largest state, and bigger than Texas, California and Montana put together. Always check an inset's scale.

blocks.html: Some places are so special that the whole country decided to protect them: giant canyons, geysers, volcanoes, caves and swamps. Many of them are national parks.

A national park protects land, water, plants and animals for everyone, now and in the future. Yellowstone became the first national park in 1872. The National Park Service, created in 1916, runs the parks. There are more than 60 national parks.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: A few national parks, from Yellowstone, the first, to the Everglades.

blocks.html: Why protect land this way? In the 1800s, people saw forests cut down, wild animals hunted out and beautiful places fenced off for private profit. The law that made Yellowstone a park in 1872 set it aside "as a public park or pleasuring-ground for the benefit and enjoyment of the people." The idea that the best landscapes belong to everyone spread to many other countries.

blocks.title: How long between?
blocks.q: Yellowstone became a park in 1872, and the National Park Service was created in 1916. How many years apart is that?
steps: Subtract the earlier year from the later year.
blocks.a: 44 years. For those years, the parks had no single agency to run them.

blocks.html: Not every place with "park" in its name is a national park, and not every Park Service place is a national park either. The National Park System has more than 400 places, and most are other kinds: national monuments (like the Statue of Liberty), memorials (like the Lincoln Memorial and Mount Rushmore), historic sites, seashores and trails. Only about 60 or so are national parks.

blocks.html: Most of the oldest and largest national parks are in the West, where the government still owned most of the land when the parks were made.

Famous western parks: Yellowstone (mostly Wyoming; geysers), Yosemite (California; granite cliffs and waterfalls), Grand Canyon (Arizona), Zion and Arches (Utah), Glacier (Montana), Rocky Mountain (Colorado), Olympic and Mount Rainier (Washington), Crater Lake (Oregon), Denali (Alaska) and Hawaiʻi Volcanoes (Hawaii).

blocks.cap: Western parks and the mountain ranges around them.

blocks.html: Why are so many parks in the mountains? Mountains, volcanoes and canyons make the most dramatic scenery, and they were hard to farm or build on, so much of the land was still wild and owned by the government when people began asking to protect it. Each park protects what made its place special: Yellowstone's hot springs, Glacier's ice-carved valleys, Crater Lake's deep blue water in an old volcano.

blocks.title: Park detective
blocks.q: A park has more than 2,000 natural stone arches in red rock desert. Which park and state?
steps: Red rock desert points to the Colorado Plateau.
The park named for its arches is Arches National Park.
It is in eastern Utah.

blocks.html: People put the Grand Canyon in Colorado because the Colorado River carved it. The river is named for the state where it starts, but the canyon, and Grand Canyon National Park, are in Arizona. Yellowstone is another trap: it is mostly in Wyoming, with small parts in Montana and Idaho.

blocks.html: The East and the middle of the country have fewer national parks than the West, but they include some of the most loved, and the most visited.

Parks east of the Rockies include the Great Smoky Mountains (Tennessee and North Carolina), Acadia (Maine), the Everglades (Florida), Shenandoah (Virginia), Mammoth Cave (Kentucky), Big Bend (Texas), Hot Springs (Arkansas), Badlands (South Dakota), Gateway Arch (Missouri) and New River Gorge (West Virginia).

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: National parks of the middle and East.

blocks.html: Why are there fewer parks in the East? By the time people started making national parks, most eastern land was already owned by farmers, towns and companies. Parks like the Great Smoky Mountains and Shenandoah had to be put together from land bought piece by piece, much of it given by states and private donors. Some eastern parks are new: Gateway Arch became a national park in 2018 and New River Gorge in 2020.

blocks.title: Underground
blocks.q: Which park protects the longest known cave system in the world, and where is it?
steps: The park is named for its huge cave.
It is Mammoth Cave National Park.
It is in central Kentucky.

blocks.html: People think all the big-name parks are in the West. The most visited national park is the Great Smoky Mountains, on the border of Tennessee and North Carolina, with about 11.5 million visits in 2025, more than twice as many as any other national park. Being close to millions of people in the East helps.

blocks.html: A landmark is something easy to see and recognize that helps people know where they are. Some are built by people; some are made by nature.

Famous landmarks and their states: the Statue of Liberty (New York), Mount Rushmore (South Dakota), the Golden Gate Bridge (California), the Gateway Arch (Missouri), the Space Needle (Washington), the Alamo (Texas), Old Faithful (Wyoming) and Niagara Falls (New York).

blocks.cap: Landmarks across the country.

blocks.html: Why learn landmarks with states? Tying a picture you know to a place on the map gives your memory two hooks instead of one. If you remember the Gateway Arch stands in St. Louis on the Mississippi River, you also remember where Missouri is.

blocks.title: Where is it?
blocks.q: The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. Which state is the island part of?
steps: The island is in the harbor between New York City and New Jersey.
The water around it belongs to New Jersey, but the island itself is part of New York.
The Park Service runs it as a national monument.

blocks.html: People mix up landmarks made by people with natural ones. Mount Rushmore is a natural mountain, but the four presidents' faces were carved by people, so the landmark is a human-made sculpture. Old Faithful is a natural geyser that shoots up hot water on its own. Ask: did nature make it, or did people build or carve it?

blocks.html: In The Sun Shows the Way you saw that the Sun rises in the east. Morning reaches the East Coast first, then moves west across the country. That is why clocks are set differently in different places.
The 50 states use six time zones. From east to west: Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific, Alaska and Hawaii-Aleutian. Each zone is one hour earlier than the zone to its east.

blocks.name: gg-timezones
blocks.cap: U.S. time zones in standard time. Move the slider to change the time everywhere at once.

blocks.html: Why zones? Long ago, every town set its clocks by its own noon, when the Sun was highest. Towns a few miles apart had slightly different times, which made train schedules a mess. In 1883 the railroads agreed on a few standard zones, each about one hour of the Sun's motion wide, and later the law made them official. Everyone in a zone shares one clock time.

blocks.title: Noon in New York
blocks.q: It is 12:00 noon in New York. What time is it in Los Angeles?
steps: New York is in the Eastern zone; Los Angeles is in the Pacific zone.
Going west: Eastern to Central to Mountain to Pacific is 3 zones.
West is earlier, so subtract 3 hours: 9:00 a.m.

blocks.html: It is easy to think the West is "later." It is the other way around. The Sun rises in the East first, so Eastern clocks are ahead. When New Yorkers eat lunch, people in California are just starting their morning. Also, some states are split: most of Texas is Central, but its far western corner (El Paso) uses Mountain Time.

sources.name: Grokipedia, Time in the United States

blocks.html: You know the six time zones. Now use them to figure out the time somewhere else. You will use what you know about elapsed time.
Count the zones between the two places. Going east, add one hour for each zone. Going west, subtract one hour for each zone.

blocks.name: gg-timezones
blocks.cap: Atlanta, Denver and Seattle. Slide the time and watch all three clocks move together.

blocks.html: Why does this work? All the clocks move together: when one gains an hour, they all do. The zones only shift the starting point. So the difference between two places stays the same all day: Denver is always 2 hours behind Atlanta (when both follow the same daylight saving rules).

blocks.title: Going east
blocks.q: In January, it is 4:30 p.m. in Seattle. What time is it in Atlanta?
steps: Seattle is Pacific; Atlanta is Eastern.
Pacific to Mountain to Central to Eastern: 3 zones east.
East is later, so add 3 hours: 4:30 p.m. + 3 = 7:30 p.m.

blocks.title: A flight west
blocks.q: A plane leaves Chicago at 10:00 a.m. and flies 4 hours to Los Angeles. What time is it in Los Angeles when it lands?
steps: On Chicago's clock, it lands at 10:00 a.m. + 4 hours = 2:00 p.m.
Los Angeles is 2 zones west of Chicago (Central to Mountain to Pacific).
Subtract 2 hours: 12:00 noon.

blocks.html: The most common slip is adding when you should subtract. Check yourself with the Sun: the Sun rises in the East first, so the East is always ahead. If your answer makes a western city later than an eastern one, flip it.
In this topic, problems say "in January" so that every state is on standard time. In summer, Arizona and Hawaii do not change their clocks; the next topic shows what that does.

sources.name: Grokipedia, Time in the United States

blocks.html: Twice a year most Americans change their clocks. The time between those changes is daylight saving time.

In most states, clocks move ahead one hour at 2:00 a.m. on the second Sunday in March and back one hour on the first Sunday in November: "spring forward, fall back." Hawaii and most of Arizona stay on standard time all year (the Navajo Nation in northeastern Arizona does change).

blocks.name: gg-timezones
blocks.cap: In winter (standard time) Phoenix shows Denver's time. In summer, Phoenix shows Los Angeles's time.

blocks.html: Why move the clocks? In summer the Sun rises very early, while many people are asleep. Moving clocks ahead shifts an hour of daylight from the early morning to the evening, when more people are awake to use it. Near the tropics, like in Hawaii, day length changes little through the year, so there is little to gain. Arizona is hot in summer, and an extra hour of evening sun is not welcome there.

blocks.title: Summer in Phoenix
blocks.q: In July, it is 3:00 p.m. in Los Angeles. What time is it in Phoenix?
steps: In July, Los Angeles is on daylight saving time: 7 hours behind UTC.
Phoenix stays on standard time: also 7 hours behind UTC.
They match, so it is 3:00 p.m. in Phoenix too.

blocks.html: People think every state changes its clocks. Hawaii and most of Arizona do not. So in summer, Arizona has the same clock time as California, even though Arizona is in the Mountain zone. In winter, Arizona matches Colorado again.

blocks.html: Weather is what the air is doing today. Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years. A country as big as the United States has many climates.

The Southeast has hot, humid summers and mild winters. The North and Midwest have cold, snowy winters. The Southwest is dry. The Pacific Northwest coast is mild and rainy, and coastal California has dry summers and rainy winters. Hawaii is tropical, and much of Alaska is very cold.

blocks.name: gg-climate
blocks.cap: Two typical climates. The red line is temperature; the blue bars are rain and snow.

blocks.html: What sets a place's climate? Four big things: how far it is from the equator (farther means colder), how high it is (higher means colder), how close it is to an ocean (oceans keep coasts mild), and where mountains block or wring out rain. Earth & Space explains these climate factors in depth.

blocks.title: Read a climograph
blocks.q: On a climograph, the bars are tall in winter and almost empty in summer, and the line never drops below freezing. What kind of place is it?
steps: Winter rain and dry summers is the Mediterranean pattern.
Mild all year means it is near the ocean.
In the United States, that fits coastal California.

blocks.html: People think the farther south you go, the hotter it always is. Latitude matters, but so do oceans and height. San Francisco has cool summers because cold ocean water and fog cool the coast. Denver, a mile high, is colder than lower places at the same latitude. Mountain towns can have snow while nearby valleys are warm.

blocks.name: gg-climate
blocks.cap: Dry summers, wet winters (left); hot and dry almost all year (right).

blocks.html: Every part of the country has some kind of natural hazard. Where each kind strikes depends on the land, the oceans and the air, so geography can predict a lot.

Hurricanes strike the Gulf and Atlantic coasts. Tornadoes are most common on the central and southern plains and in the Southeast. Earthquakes are most common in Alaska, California and the rest of the West.

blocks.name: gg-sort
blocks.cap: Which hazard is each place best known for?

blocks.html: Each hazard has its own recipe. Hurricanes draw their energy from warm ocean water, so they hit coasts and weaken over land; the Atlantic hurricane season runs from June 1 to November 30. Tornadoes form in strong thunderstorms where warm, moist air from the Gulf meets cool, dry air from the West, which often happens over the plains in spring. Earthquakes happen where pieces of Earth's crust grind past each other, as they do along the Pacific edge. (See Hurricanes and Supercells and Tornadoes for the science.)

blocks.title: Which hazard?
blocks.q: Kansas is far from any ocean, on flat plains in the middle of the country. Which hazard is it best known for?
steps: Hurricanes need warm ocean water, so they rarely reach Kansas.
Earthquakes are rare there too.
Spring storms on the plains often make tornadoes.

blocks.html: People think tornadoes happen only in one "Tornado Alley." Tornadoes have been reported in every state. "Tornado Alley" is only a nickname, not an exact area, for the central plains where tornadoes are most frequent; the Southeast also gets many, often at night. Similarly, the U.S. Geological Survey calls Alaska the most earthquake-prone state, yet small earthquakes happen in many states.

blocks.html: Every ten years the Census Bureau counts everyone in the country. The 2020 Census tells us which cities are the biggest. To compare their populations you will use comparing large numbers.

In the 2020 Census, the five largest U.S. cities were New York (about 8.8 million people), Los Angeles (about 3.9 million), Chicago (about 2.7 million), Houston (about 2.3 million) and Phoenix (about 1.6 million).

blocks.html: Why did these cities grow so big? Most grew where travel was easy: New York on a great harbor, Chicago where the Great Lakes meet railroads, Houston near the Gulf. Later, many people moved to the warm South and West, so Phoenix, San Antonio and Dallas grew fast in the last fifty years.

blocks.title: Compare two cities
blocks.q: Which had more people in 2020: Phoenix (1,608,139) or Philadelphia (1,603,797)?
steps: Both have 7 digits, and both start with 1,60.
Compare the thousands: 608 thousand is more than 603 thousand.
So Phoenix had a little more.

blocks.html: People assume a state's biggest city is its capital. Of the ten largest cities in 2020, only Phoenix is a state capital. New York's capital is Albany, California's is Sacramento, Illinois's is Springfield, and Texas's is Austin (the 11th largest city).

blocks.html: States differ hugely in how many people live in them. The largest cities help explain why.

In the 2020 Census, the states with the most people were California (about 39.5 million), Texas (about 29.1 million), Florida (about 21.5 million), New York (about 20.2 million) and Pennsylvania (about 13.0 million). Wyoming had the fewest, about 577,000.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Population of each state in 2020. Read the key to see which color means more people.

blocks.html: Why do people cluster in some states? People settle where they can make a living: near ports and rivers for trade, on good farmland, and in places with jobs. Big cities draw more people, which brings more jobs. Mild weather has pulled many people to Florida, Texas and California. Mountains, deserts and cold, as in Wyoming or Alaska, keep numbers low.

blocks.title: Round to the nearest million
blocks.q: Texas had 29,145,505 people in 2020. What is that to the nearest million?
steps: The millions digit is 9, so the choices are 29 million and 30 million.
Look at the hundred-thousands digit: 1.
1 is less than 5, so round down.

blocks.html: People think the biggest states by area have the most people. Alaska is the largest state, yet only Wyoming, Vermont (and the District of Columbia) had fewer people in 2020. Area and population are different things: one measures land, the other counts people.

sources.name: U.S. Census Bureau, 2020 Census apportionment results: resident population and population density by state (table as republished by the New Jersey Department of Labor)

blocks.html: How crowded is a state? Total population does not tell you, because states have very different amounts of land. California has the most people, but it also has a lot of room.

Population density = people ÷ land area. It tells how many people there are for each square mile. In 2020, New Jersey was the most crowded state (about 1,263 people per square mile) and Alaska the least (about 1.3).

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: Population density by state, from the Census Bureau.

blocks.html: Density is a unit rate: the number of people for one square mile. Dividing by area makes states of different sizes fair to compare, the same way price per ounce lets you compare a small box and a big box of cereal.

blocks.title: Find a density
blocks.q: Rhode Island had about 1,100,000 people on about 1,000 square miles of land. What was its density?
steps: Density = people ÷ land area.
About 1,100 people per square mile.
blocks.a: About 1,100 people per square mile (the Census Bureau's exact figure is about 1,061).

blocks.title: More people, less crowded
blocks.q: Texas had about 29,000,000 people on about 261,000 square miles. Is it more crowded than Rhode Island?
steps: 29,000,000 ÷ 261,000 ≈ 111 people per square mile.
Rhode Island has about 1,061.
Texas has far more people, but far more land, so it is less crowded.
blocks.a: No. Texas is about one tenth as crowded.

blocks.html: People compare total population when the question is about crowding. Density divides people by land area, so a small state with fewer people, like Rhode Island, can be much more crowded than a big state with many people, like Texas.

blocks.html: The United States grows a huge share of the world's food. But not every crop grows everywhere. Farmers grow what the climate and soil of their land suit best.

Leaders: Iowa and Illinois in corn (and soybeans), Kansas and North Dakota in wheat, Texas in cotton and cattle, Idaho in potatoes, California in fruits, nuts and vegetables, Washington in apples and Wisconsin in milk and cheese.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: A few states and the crop each one is best known for. Most states grow many crops.

blocks.html: Why does each crop have its place? Corn needs warm, wet summers and deep soil, like the Central Lowland's. Wheat needs less rain, so it fits the drier Great Plains. Oranges die in hard freezes, so they grow where winters are mild, like Florida and California. Potatoes do well in Idaho's volcanic soil, with cool nights and river water for irrigation. Climate and soil decide; farmers follow.

blocks.title: The Corn Belt
blocks.q: Why are Iowa and Illinois the top corn states, and not Nevada?
steps: Corn needs a lot of summer rain and warm days.
Iowa and Illinois have hot, wet summers and deep, rich soil.
Nevada is a desert, too dry for corn without irrigation.
blocks.a: Their climate and soil suit corn.

blocks.html: People think one state grows everything. Crops follow climate and soil, so each region has its specialties. Rankings also shift from year to year: Kansas and North Dakota trade first place in wheat, and in 2022 North Dakota led.

blocks.html: The United States began with thirteen states along the Atlantic coast. Each had been a British colony before the Revolution.

The thirteen original states were New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. Delaware was the first to approve the Constitution, on December 7, 1787; Rhode Island was the last of the thirteen, in 1790.

blocks.name: gg-map
blocks.cap: The thirteen original states (orange) and their later neighbors.

blocks.html: Why are they all on the Atlantic? European colonists arrived by ship across the Atlantic, so the first settlements were on the coast and along rivers that ships could sail up. Towns, farms and colonies spread inland from there. The order of joining is the order in which each state's convention approved the Constitution.

blocks.title: One of the thirteen?
blocks.q: Was Vermont one of the thirteen original states?
steps: Vermont is in New England, near the thirteen.
But it was not one of the colonies; it joined later.
It became the 14th state in 1791.

blocks.html: People include Vermont or Maine because they are in New England. Neither was one of the thirteen: Vermont became the 14th state in 1791, and Maine was part of Massachusetts until it became a state in 1820. West Virginia split from Virginia in 1863.

blocks.html: After the first thirteen states, the country grew in big pieces. The 1783 peace treaty with Britain set the western border at the Mississippi River. After that, land was added in several large steps.

The big additions: the Louisiana Purchase (1803, from France), Florida (1819 treaty with Spain), Texas (1845, annexed), the Oregon Country (1846, divided with Britain), the Mexican Cession (1848, from Mexico after the U.S.-Mexican War), the Gadsden Purchase (1853, from Mexico), Alaska (1867, from Russia) and Hawaii (1898, annexed).

blocks.name: gg-map

opts.legend: Most of the state came from

blocks.cap: Each state colored by the addition most of its land came from. The additions' borders do not follow today's state lines; states left plain (Minnesota, Colorado, Wyoming, Arizona and New Mexico) came from two or more.

blocks.html: Why in big pieces? Each piece came from a single agreement with whoever held the land: a purchase from France or Russia, a treaty with Spain or Britain, Texas and Hawaii agreeing to join, or the treaty that ended a war with Mexico. One agreement could move a border hundreds of miles. American Indian nations already lived on all of these lands, and their own treaties with the United States are another part of this history.

blocks.title: In order
blocks.q: Put these in order: Alaska, the Louisiana Purchase, the Mexican Cession.
steps: Louisiana Purchase: 1803.
Mexican Cession: 1848.
Alaska: 1867.

blocks.html: People picture the country growing west one thin strip at a time. It grew in big pieces, by purchases, treaties, annexations and a war, and not always from east to west. The Louisiana Purchase reached the Rocky Mountains in 1803, and Alaska was added in 1867, more than twenty years before Washington, Montana or the Dakotas became states.

blocks.html: After the thirteen, new states joined one at a time, each by an act of Congress, as people settled the lands the country added. The last two joined in 1959.
Delaware was first (1787) and Hawaii last (1959). Eastern states mostly joined early; many western states joined around 1890 (six in 1889 and 1890 alone); Alaska and Hawaii both joined in 1959.

blocks.cap: When each state joined. Notice the jumps: Texas and California joined long before their neighbors.

blocks.html: Why didn't the states join neatly from east to west? A territory could ask to become a state when enough people lived there and they wrote a state constitution that Congress accepted. Gold, ports and farmland drew people to some places much earlier than others. The California Gold Rush brought so many people that California joined in 1850, while the dry lands between it and Texas filled in slowly.

blocks.title: Years apart
blocks.q: Delaware became a state in 1787 and Hawaii in 1959. How many years apart is that?
steps: Subtract: 1959 − 1787.

blocks.html: People think states joined in order from east to west. Texas (1845) and California (1850) joined decades before nearby states such as Nevada (1864), Utah (1896), New Mexico and Arizona (both 1912). Oklahoma came in 1907, and Alaska and Hawaii came last, both in 1959.
